title: Climate and Monsoon - India and Andhra Pradesh
intake_rule: Each printed page was read visually from its rendered image once. Printed prose, tables, boxes, maps, diagrams and PYQs are recorded before note or MCQ authoring; handwritten marks are ignored.
table_policy: Every printed table is preserved cell-by-cell. Verified corrections are labelled separately and dated; concepts remain prose while comparisons and datasets remain responsive semantic tables.

pages.heading: India's monsoon climate and four seasons

facts.claim: Climate is the long-term pattern of temperature, pressure, winds, humidity and precipitation over a region.
India extends roughly from 8°4′N to 37°6′N and 68°7′E to 97°25′E; the book's rounded coordinates require correction to standard official values.
The Tropic of Cancer crosses India and helps divide tropical southern India from subtropical northern India, although relief and monsoon circulation complicate this simple latitudinal division.
India is commonly described as having a tropical monsoon climate with strong regional variation caused by latitude, altitude, relief, distance from the sea and monsoon circulation.
The word monsoon is associated with the Arabic word mausim, meaning season, and refers to a seasonal reversal or marked seasonal change in prevailing winds.
Summer heating creates lower pressure over the subcontinent and helps draw moisture-bearing winds from the surrounding oceans; winter cooling reverses the broad pressure contrast.
Monsoon onset, duration, withdrawal and rainfall amount vary from place to place and from year to year.
The book divides the Indian annual weather cycle into hot-weather, southwest-monsoon, retreating or northeast-monsoon, and cold-weather seasons.
The hot-weather season begins as the Sun's apparent northward movement intensifies land heating; extreme temperatures occur in parts of northwestern and central India.
Specific annual temperature records printed for 2024 are time-sensitive and must be dated and verified before scoring.

pages.heading: Hot-weather season, loo and pre-monsoon storms

facts.claim: During the hot-weather season, temperatures generally rise from south to north over much of India, while peninsular coasts remain more equable because of maritime influence.
The book lists representative May temperatures for Chennai, Mumbai, Delhi and Rajasthan; these are climatological examples, not universal daily maxima, and require source-year labelling.
Northwestern India's intense summer heat creates low pressure that contributes to the developing monsoon circulation.
Loo winds are strong, hot and dry winds that blow over the northern plains during late spring and early summer, often in the afternoon.
Dust storms and thunderstorms may temporarily lower temperature and produce brief rain during the hot-weather season.
Blossom showers are pre-monsoon showers associated especially with coffee-growing areas of Karnataka and Kerala.
Mango showers are pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka that assist early ripening of mangoes; usage sometimes extends to adjoining southern regions.
Nor'westers are violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms over eastern and northeastern India, especially West Bengal and Assam; in Bengal they are called Kalbaisakhi.
The printed Group-I question asks where snowfall is continuous; the preserved answer is Srinagar, but the wording and official key require source-paper verification before scoring.
The southwest monsoon normally advances from the equatorial Indian Ocean toward Kerala near the beginning of June, but the onset date varies annually.

pages.heading: Advancing southwest monsoon and its branches

facts.claim: The southwest monsoon is also called the advancing monsoon or hot-wet season and is the main rainy season for most of India.
Cross-equatorial southeasterly trade winds turn southwesterly after crossing the equator because of the Coriolis effect and pressure distribution.
The monsoon reaches the Kerala coast near early June in a normal year and advances northward in two principal branches: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal.
The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Western Ghats, producing heavy orographic rainfall on the windward west coast and a rain-shadow effect over parts of the Deccan interior.
The Bay of Bengal branch moves toward northeastern India and the Ganga plain, where relief and the monsoon trough influence its path.
Mawsynram and Cherrapunji receive exceptionally heavy rainfall because moisture-bearing winds are forced up the funnel-shaped Khasi Hills terrain.
Rainfall generally decreases westward along the northern plains as the Bay of Bengal branch progressively loses moisture.
The book states that about 75% of India's annual rainfall occurs in the southwest-monsoon season; the exact national share varies by dataset and period.
The advancing-monsoon map shows approximate isochrones and branches; it is schematic and annual onset dates are not fixed boundaries.

pages.heading: Monsoon onset, burst, breaks and rainfall distribution

facts.claim: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone shifts northward over the subcontinent in summer and is expressed regionally as the monsoon trough.
Heating of the Tibetan Plateau and changes in upper-air circulation contribute to the seasonal development of the South Asian monsoon.
The southwest monsoon normally reaches the Andaman-Nicobar region in the second half of May, Kerala near 1 June and much of India by mid-July; dates vary annually.
Monsoon burst refers to the sudden onset of sustained heavy rain after the pre-monsoon season.
A break in the monsoon is a temporary weakening or interruption of rainfall over large areas during the rainy season, often linked to shifts in the monsoon trough.
Southwest-monsoon rainfall generally decreases from Kolkata toward Delhi and from the west coast toward the Deccan interior, but local relief produces exceptions.
Rain-shadow areas occur leeward of mountain barriers where descending air is relatively drier after windward uplift and precipitation.
Cloud seeding attempts to enhance precipitation by introducing suitable particles into clouds; results depend on cloud conditions and it cannot create rain from a cloudless sky.
The book's city rainfall examples are approximate climatological figures and require a named period and official dataset before use as scored exact values.

facts.claim: The southwest monsoon begins withdrawing from northwestern India around September and retreats progressively southeastward.
The retreating-monsoon season is associated with the southward shift of the monsoon trough and changing land-sea pressure patterns.
During October-November, depressions and cyclones over the Bay of Bengal can bring heavy rain to the Coromandel coast and southeastern peninsula.
Tamil Nadu receives a major share of its annual rainfall during the northeast-monsoon or retreating-monsoon season.
The cold-weather season extends broadly from December to February, with lower temperatures in northern India and milder conditions in the peninsula.
Western disturbances are extratropical weather systems that bring winter precipitation to northwestern India and snowfall to the western Himalaya.
Winter precipitation from western disturbances is important for rabi crops, but excessive or untimely events may damage crops.
The printed withdrawal map and timetable are schematic normals; recent IMD withdrawal criteria and dates must be used for corrections.

pages.heading: Annual rainfall regions and seasonal rainfall shares

facts.claim: India's mean annual rainfall is commonly stated near 116-120 cm depending on dataset and period; the book gives 118/120 cm.
Very high rainfall occurs on the windward Western Ghats, in parts of northeastern India and in the Andaman-Nicobar region.
Moderate rainfall covers much of the northern plains and central-eastern India, while low and very low rainfall characterize rain-shadow interiors and the arid northwest.
Cherrapunji and Mawsynram are often cited for exceptionally high annual rainfall, while western Rajasthan is among India's driest regions; exact station normals must be period-labelled.
The book distributes India's annual rainfall as 75% southwest monsoon, 13% retreating monsoon, 10% hot-weather season and 2% winter; these are broad textbook shares.
The annual-rainfall map uses broad classes greater than 200 cm, 100-200 cm, 50-100 cm and less than 50 cm.
India's rainfall is highly variable in time and space; a national mean does not describe every location.

pages.heading: Drought, traditional monsoon names and climatic controls

facts.claim: The book states that about 12% of India's area is drought-prone and refers to a national drought-mitigation programme begun in 1954; both the percentage and programme terminology require official verification.

The book distinguishes severe drought where normal rainfall is deficient by at least 50% and drought where deficiency is at least 25%; modern IMD rainfall-deficiency categories use specific thresholds and terminology that must be applied.

Drought-prone regions include western Rajasthan and parts of Gujarat, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab, Bihar and Odisha, but district boundaries and classifications change with methodology.
Rainfall variability and drought risk are generally greater in low-rainfall regions than in consistently wet regions.
Thermal contrast between the Asian landmass and surrounding oceans is one factor in monsoon circulation, but it is not a complete explanation by itself.
India's latitudinal extent, the Tropic of Cancer and surrounding seas help explain regional climate differences.
Relief controls rainfall by forcing moist air upward on windward slopes and creating rain shadows on leeward slopes.
The Himalaya restricts cold continental air from entering India and helps block the northward escape of monsoon winds.
Seasonal migration of the ITCZ helps organize monsoon wind and rainfall belts.

pages.heading: Monsoon controls: relief, ITCZ, jet streams, El Nino and La Nina

facts.claim: Mountain orientation and gaps affect monsoon penetration and rainfall distribution; windward and leeward positions are crucial.
The ITCZ is a low-pressure convergence belt near the thermal equator whose seasonal movement contributes to monsoon circulation.
The subtropical westerly jet lies south of the Himalaya in winter and shifts north in summer, while a tropical easterly jet develops over the upper troposphere during the summer monsoon.
The book's printed jet-stream altitude, speed and latitude ranges are approximate and need verification from meteorological sources.
El Nino is the warm phase of ENSO, characterized by anomalous warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific with coupled atmospheric changes.
El Nino often weakens the Indian summer monsoon statistically, but the relationship is not deterministic and individual years vary.
La Nina is the cool phase of ENSO, characterized by below-average equatorial Pacific sea-surface temperatures and strengthened trade-wind circulation.
La Nina is often associated with stronger Indian monsoon rainfall statistically, but other ocean-atmosphere factors can modify the outcome.

pages.heading: El Nino Modoki, Southern Oscillation, ENSO and Indian Ocean Dipole

facts.claim: El Nino Modoki refers to a central-Pacific warming pattern distinct from the classic eastern-Pacific El Nino; its impacts depend on the event pattern and season.
The Southern Oscillation is a large-scale seesaw in tropical Pacific sea-level pressure, commonly monitored using Tahiti and Darwin pressure differences.
ENSO is the coupled ocean-atmosphere system combining El Nino or La Nina sea-surface temperature anomalies with Southern Oscillation pressure and wind changes.
Sir Gilbert Walker investigated the Southern Oscillation while studying Indian monsoon variability; the associated zonal tropical circulation is called Walker circulation.
The Indian Ocean Dipole is a mode of coupled ocean-atmosphere variability involving an east-west sea-surface temperature gradient across the tropical Indian Ocean.
A positive IOD has relatively warmer western and cooler eastern tropical Indian Ocean conditions; a negative IOD has the opposite sign.
IOD and ENSO can interact in influencing Indian monsoon rainfall, but neither alone determines seasonal rainfall everywhere.
The printed diagram contrasts normal and anomalous Walker-circulation flow and marks Darwin, Tahiti and the El Nino current region.

pages.heading: Mascarene High and theories of monsoon origin

facts.claim: The Mascarene High is a subtropical high-pressure cell over the southern Indian Ocean that supports cross-equatorial flow toward the South Asian summer monsoon.
Its position and strength vary seasonally; it is one component of the monsoon circulation rather than a single-cause explanation.
Edmond Halley proposed an early thermal theory linking monsoon wind reversal to differential heating of land and sea.
Flohn emphasized seasonal shifts in planetary circulation and the equatorial westerlies in explaining monsoon behavior.
The Tibetan Plateau's elevated heating can influence upper-air circulation, pressure fields and the tropical easterly jet.
Krishnamurti and other dynamic meteorologists examined upper-air circulation, monsoon depressions and jet-stream mechanisms.
Ramanathan, Ramaswamy and other Indian meteorologists contributed observational and dynamical studies of monsoon circulation; individual printed attributions require source verification.
International monsoon experiments used ships, aircraft, balloons, satellites and ground observations to study air-sea-land interactions.

pages.heading: Monsoon experiments, rainfall variability and Koppen classification

facts.claim: The book lists ISMEX and Monsoon-77 among international monsoon experiments; acronyms, dates and participating programmes require documentary verification.
MONEX-1979 was a major component of the Global Atmospheric Research Programme's First GARP Global Experiment focused on the monsoon system.
The printed expressions World Wealth Watch and WAMEX-1979 require correction or verification; they must not be scored until confirmed.
Rainfall deviation compares an observed seasonal or annual total with its long-period normal, while rainfall variability describes how values fluctuate across years.
Coefficient of variation is calculated as standard deviation divided by mean, multiplied by 100.
Low-rainfall regions usually have a higher coefficient of variation than high-rainfall regions, so their rainfall is less reliable.
Wladimir Koppen developed and revised an empirical climate classification based mainly on temperature, precipitation and vegetation relationships.
Koppen's major groups are A tropical, B dry, C temperate or mild mid-latitude, D continental or cold mid-latitude, and E polar; exact threshold wording must follow the modern scheme used.

pages.heading: Koppen letter codes and Indian climate regions

facts.claim: Within dry climates, S denotes steppe or semi-arid and W denotes desert or arid conditions.
Within polar climates, ET denotes tundra and EF denotes ice-cap climate; the book prints T and F as secondary letters.

Lowercase letters describe seasonal precipitation or temperature characteristics: f no dry season, w dry winter, s dry summer, with additional thermal letters such as a, b, c, d or h depending on the group.
The book's printed meanings for g, h and m reflect an older Indian textbook adaptation and must be reconciled with the exact Koppen variant used.
Am or Amw denotes tropical monsoon climate with a short dry season in older Indian mappings, concentrated along very wet coastal and northeastern areas.
As represents a tropical climate with a dry summer in the printed scheme and occurs in a limited southeastern coastal zone; code usage varies across map editions.
Aw denotes tropical savanna with a dry winter and covers large parts of peninsular and central India in the printed map.
BShw denotes semi-arid steppe with dry winter in the older map, covering parts of the Deccan rain shadow and northwestern transition zone.

pages.heading: Koppen regions of India and Thornthwaite classification basis

facts.claim: BWhw denotes hot desert climate in the older map and occupies western Rajasthan and adjoining arid areas.
Cwg denotes a monsoon-influenced mild climate with dry winter in the printed map, covering much of the northern plains and adjoining uplands.
Dfc is shown over limited high northeastern or Himalayan terrain as a cold humid climate with short summer; modern classifications may use different codes and boundaries.
ET tundra climate occurs at high Himalayan elevations where the warmest month remains cool; EF ice-cap climate is confined to permanent snow and ice zones.
The printed Koppen map is a simplified historical scheme and its regions should not be treated as precise current district boundaries.
C. W. Thornthwaite classified climates using moisture balance, especially precipitation effectiveness and potential evapotranspiration.
Thornthwaite first published a climate classification in 1931 and substantially revised it in 1948; the book also mentions 1955, which requires context verification.

visuals: Simplified Koppen climatic-regions map of India

facts.claim: The printed Thornthwaite scheme divides India into perhumid A, humid B, moist sub-humid C2, dry sub-humid C1, semi-arid D and arid E regions.
Perhumid regions are concentrated in very wet areas such as the windward Western Ghats, northeastern India and island sectors.
Humid and moist sub-humid zones include parts of eastern and coastal India, while dry sub-humid and semi-arid zones occupy much of the interior.
Arid conditions dominate western Rajasthan and adjoining desert areas.
The map is schematic and category boundaries depend on the climatic period, water-balance method and spatial resolution used.

pages.heading: Climate of Andhra Pradesh and four seasons

facts.claim: Andhra Pradesh lies between the Bay of Bengal coast and interior plateau-upland regions, producing strong maritime-to-continental and relief contrasts.
Most of Andhra Pradesh has a tropical climate, with coastal humidity, hot summers and rainfall from both southwest and northeast monsoons.
The book states that about 23% of the state's area is hilly; this figure requires an identified state dataset and boundary year.
Mean temperatures are higher in the plains and lower in elevated areas such as the Eastern Ghats and interior uplands.
May is generally the hottest month over much of Andhra Pradesh, while coastal areas have smaller daily and annual temperature ranges than inland Rayalaseema.
Local extreme-temperature records printed for individual districts are time-sensitive and must be dated and verified before scoring.
Andhra Pradesh is described through four seasonal periods: hot weather, southwest monsoon, northeast monsoon and winter.
Pre-monsoon thunderstorms may bring strong winds, hail and short intense rain in parts of the state.

pages.heading: Andhra Pradesh southwest and northeast monsoon seasons

facts.claim: The southwest monsoon normally reaches Andhra Pradesh in early June, but onset timing varies by year and by coastal-interior location.
The book states that roughly three-fourths of Andhra Pradesh's annual rainfall falls during the southwest monsoon; the share differs markedly across districts and official climatological periods.
The Arabian Sea branch and Bay of Bengal systems both affect the state, while rain-shadow effects reduce rainfall over parts of Rayalaseema.
The northeast monsoon or retreating-monsoon season is especially important for coastal Andhra Pradesh and southern districts from October to December.
Bay of Bengal depressions and cyclones are major sources of heavy northeast-monsoon rain and coastal hazards.
Cyclone landfall frequency, deaths and individual historical records printed in the book are time-sensitive and require an IMD disaster archive before scoring.
Winter is generally mild and dry, with cooler nights over inland and elevated areas.
The Lambasingi region is popularly described as one of Andhra Pradesh's coldest locations, but exact minimum-temperature claims require station metadata and official observations.

pages.heading: Andhra Pradesh rainfall totals and district extremes

facts.claim: The book gives Andhra Pradesh mean annual rainfall as 966 mm, while other official periods may report different state averages; every value must carry its reference period.
Rainfall is uneven across the state, with generally wetter northern-coastal and Eastern-Ghat sectors and drier Rayalaseema interiors.
Year-to-year variability is high, and drought and flood can occur in different parts of the state within the same broad season.
The book's 2008-2018 statement and 2010-11 rainfall maximum are period-specific statistics that require verification from the Andhra Pradesh statistical abstract.
During the southwest monsoon, coastal districts generally receive more rain than the Rayalaseema rain-shadow interior, though local relief and cyclone tracks create exceptions.
The printed district maxima and minima for southwest-monsoon rainfall use a historical district map and must be translated carefully to the current 26-district structure.
During the northeast monsoon, the coast and southern districts receive substantial rain, while interior western districts are generally drier.
Printed extreme district values are source-year dependent and must remain unscored until an official period and boundary system are attached.

pages.heading: Seasonal rainfall and Andhra Pradesh climate classifications

facts.claim: The book gives winter mean rainfall near 15.7 mm and lists district extremes; these period-specific figures require an official source and district-boundary year.
The book gives hot-weather-season mean rainfall near 98.3 mm and lists district extremes; these values are period-specific.
In the printed Koppen scheme, parts of the south coast are mapped as As, much of central and northern Andhra Pradesh as Aw, and the drier Rayalaseema interior as BShw.
In the printed Thornthwaite scheme, Andhra Pradesh is predominantly semi-arid, with dry sub-humid, moist sub-humid and arid zones also represented.
The Andhra Pradesh annual-rainfall map uses three broad classes: more than 100 cm, 60-99 cm and less than 60 cm.
The printed map is based on an older district outline and must be treated as a rainfall-zone map rather than a current administrative map.
Climate classification boundaries are transitional and depend on the thresholds, data period and spatial resolution of the scheme used.
